content_metadata.description: The video discusses the vulnerability of Deep Neural Networks to out-of-distribution (OOD) data, evaluates existing approaches, and introduces the Guaranteed Out-Of-Distribution Detection (GOOD) method, highlighting its advantages.

qAndA.question: What is the confidence score of the standard model on the chimpanzee image before any manipulation?
What is the confidence score of the GOOD model on the slightly manipulated chimpanzee image on the right?
What does "GOOD" stand for in this presentation?
What is the maximum confidence score that GOOD guarantees for any OOD input within a specific perturbation radius around the chimpanzee image?

qAndA.answer: Real-world scenarios often involve encountering data from distributions that were not present during training.
qAndA.question: Why is it important for OOD detection methods to generalize to unseen distributions?

scenes.contextualRelevance: Introduction of a technical problem and a proposed solution

narrativeProgression.description: Problem statement: Deep Neural Networks misclassify OOD inputs with high confidence.
Existing approaches (OE) reduce OOD confidence but are still vulnerable to perturbations.
Proposed solution: GOOD method provides guarantees on low confidence for OOD data, even under perturbations.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Hello and welcome to the presentation of the paper on certifiably adversarily
robust detection of all of the distribution data that I did together with Alex
Mankke and Matthias Haien at Uni tubing in. When we have a deep neural network
classifier for C410, there is trained for distinguishing dogs and mine other
classes like cats and chips and we now feed an input into this classifier that
does not belong to any of these classes, like to simply see here on the right.
Then the model is often still very confident that it classifies this input correctly,
like here it is 100% certain that the chimpanzee is a dog. We call such inputs out of
distribution, short OOD, and by confidence we mean the highest predicted
probability in any of the classes. One problem with such high confidence
predictions is that the model does not recognize that it operates outside of
its specification and should trigger human intervention or for example if it's
the self-driving vehicle it should better slow down. Now there are approaches like
outlay exposure that produce models that do have low confidence on OOD inputs but
for those models it can still be possible to construct imperceptible perturbations,
to have it images like the slightly manipulated chimpanzee here on the right.
Where even outlay exposure has 100% confidence. What we now aim to do is to guarantee
that no such high confidence perturbation exists and for this we regard the context of an
L infinity threat model which means that each individual pixel value can be changed by up to a
certain epsilon to maximize confidence and then we look at the worst confidence that can occur
this way. Using interval bound propagation we derive mathematical upper bounds on the
confidence and then during training we minimize those upper bounds on OOD inputs and at the same
time we keep the cross entropy loss on the indistribution. What we get from this procedure are
good models that indeed provide low confidence guarantees on many kinds of OOD inputs and those
guarantees even generalize to new distributions that have never been seen during training.
While other programmable robustness methods severely worsen test error with good there is almost
no drop in indistribution accuracy. Finally regarding the quality of the guarantees
the guarantees are often better than worst case samples we can find for standard methods.
For example we can guarantee that no small perturbation increases the confidence of good
on this chimpanzee above 22.7%.
